h:
Kingdom Code has been making a specific forensic argument: the Western canon was narrowed by institutional decisions that served Roman imperial interests, not apostolic preservation. The Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees, texts that explain what the Western Bible assumes you already know, were removed. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which received the apostolic faith in 34 AD before Rome had any theological hand in it, never removed them.

So I asked someone inside that tradition specific questions.

She was born in Addis Ababa and comes from a very Orthodox family. Her name is Veronica.

The Questions.

Rocka: The 81-book canon. Growing up, was it just assumed as normal? Did you know other Christians were reading something different?

Veronica: “Yes, the 81-book canon is our baseline. We knew the Catholics had 73 books and Protestants had 66 and viewed them as truncated versions of the full narrative.”

Truncated. Not different. Not alternative. Incomplete.

That’s the view from inside the tradition that never lost the texts. You’re not reading a different Bible. You’re reading a shorter one.

Rocka: The Book of Enoch specifically. Scripture or background knowledge?

Veronica: “Yes, the Book of Enoch was always recognized as Scripture and included in our Bibles. But not really discussed and probably taken for granted.”

Taken for granted.

Western Christianity has spent decades debating whether Enoch belongs in the canon. Scholars write books about it. Theologians argue about its authority.

In Ethiopia it’s the cheap Bible at the open air market. It’s assumed. It’s background. Nobody debates whether it belongs because it was never removed.

The treasure was never buried. You just weren’t given the map.

Rocka: Why isn’t Enoch preached on Sundays if it’s recognized as Scripture?

Veronica: “We rarely hear sermons on Enoch because it doesn’t lend itself to feel-good or prosperity-driven messaging. The mainstream Orthodox church, believe it or not, is like any other and has become Pharisaical, prioritizing its own preservation over serving the community. Doubt Jesus would approve.”

The canon is intact. The institution is still an institution. Having the right texts doesn’t automatically produce faithful transmission of what those texts contain. The Ethiopian Orthodox church preserved Enoch in its Bible for two thousand years and still found a way to avoid preaching it.

Because institutions everywhere protect themselves first. The content that challenges institutional comfort gets quietly sidelined regardless of whether it’s in the canon or not.

The preservation is real. The institutional capture is also real. Both things are true simultaneously. Western Christianity lost the texts. Ethiopian Christianity kept the texts and found other ways to avoid them.

Rocka: The Kebra Nagast. You called it propaganda. Explain.

Veronica: “The Kebra Nagast was essentially the monarchy’s way of justifying its right to rule. They leveraged the average Ethiopian’s soft spot for Christianity to tether political authority to a biblical lineage.”

This is the correction Kingdom Code needed before publishing any piece that uses the Kebra Nagast as primary evidence.

It’s the Ethiopian version of the divine right of kings. A royal legitimacy document dressed in sacred history. Useful for understanding Ethiopian national identity. Not the same as the 81-book canon itself.

The distinction matters. The canon preservation argument doesn’t rest on the Kebra Nagast. It rests on what’s in the Bible at the open air market. Those are separate claims and she separated them clearly.

Rocka: What does Western Christianity consistently get wrong about Ethiopian Orthodoxy?

Veronica: “Westerners seem to romanticize Ethiopian Orthodoxy as ‘pure,’ projecting an idyllic spirituality onto it. In reality, the modern institution is as flawed and commercialized as any other. Lalibela and the traditions of the northern countryside are different and may actually live up to that ideal. (Conversation for another day).”

The romanticization problem is real and Kingdom Code is not immune to it.

The argument isn’t that Ethiopia is a perfect uncorrupted spiritual paradise. The argument is that a specific textual preservation happened there that didn’t happen anywhere else. The institution is flawed. The canon is intact. Those are different things and conflating them weakens the forensic argument.

Lalibela is now on the research list.

Rocka: Western Christians discover the 81-book canon, what’s that like from your side?

Veronica: “We don’t really think about the West discovering our canon. Most Ethiopians are pretty solipsistic in that way and don’t pay much attention to what the rest of the world is doing or what they think they’ve found.”

Ethiopia isn’t waiting for Western validation. They’re not tracking what Kingdom Code publishes about their canon. They’re not monitoring whether Western scholars are finally catching up. They’ve been reading the same Bible for two thousand years and the rest of the world’s discovery timeline is not their concern.

That’s the posture of a tradition that never lost what others are just finding. You don’t celebrate someone discovering something you never misplaced.

Rocka: Ethiopian Orthodoxy survived Rome, Islam, the Ottomans, and colonial Europe with its canon intact. Does that feel significant from inside the tradition?

Veronica: “Yes, Ethiopians are a pretty proud people and independence is central to that pride. But being one of the first to adopt Christianity is probably our biggest flex.”

34 AD. The Ethiopian eunuch on the road from Jerusalem. Philip explaining Isaiah in a chariot. Baptism on the side of the road. The faith carried back to Africa before Rome had any hand in it.

That’s the flex. Not the preservation. The reception.

They were first. Everything else follows from that.

What Western Christianity is still discovering, Ethiopia took for granted two thousand years ago.

The texts were never lost in Addis. They were just missing from your translation.

The question Kingdom Code keeps asking isn’t whether Enoch belongs in the canon. It’s why someone needed you to never find out it did.

Ethiopia never had to ask that question.

They never gave anyone the chance to make it disappear.
